rows.en: And as most of his teaching is the teaching of the Pharisees, so too his religious position did not differ in essentials from the position of the Pharisees. However, it was the custom of the Pharisees from of old not to swerve even a step from the accepted beliefs and opinions and from the principles of the religion of their Torah, the first of which is complete unity; and although the belief in the coming of our righteous Messiah was engraved on the tablet of the heart of every man of Israel and sustained them in all the hardships of their lives, nevertheless, if one or another arose among them to say, "I am the chosen one whom God has sent," they did not hasten to believe that he was the one for whom their eyes were always waiting. And indeed, not many days passed before a new change was revealed within their community. Then the members of the sect became two camps. The one camp remained in the position of the Jewish religion, and the second abolished the Torah of Moses with respect to its practical part. The leader of the second was Paul, whose Hebrew name was Saul and who claimed to be a disciple of Rabban Gamaliel the Elder. He set aside the practical commandments and made the belief in their Messiah and in his resurrection after death the principal thing, and he strove to show that all this is hinted at in Holy Scripture according to the ways of the midrash of the sages. The second prevailed over the first, and in the course of time the Messianic Jews came to an end, and the religion of the Messianists was a new one, which its first founder had not imagined. For the first founder said explicitly that he was sent to the Jews (Matt. 10:6) and did not come to uproot the Torah but to fulfil it (ibid. 5:17); and he said that although the chief thing is the commandment of righteousness and love, nevertheless it is fitting not to let go of the practice (ibid. 23:23; Luke 11:42). And he took care in every way not to give his opponents a pretext, lest they say that he came to uproot the Torah, and he explicitly commanded his followers to be careful in keeping the practice (Matt. 5:4).⚠1 And if he permitted some prohibition among the prohibitions of the Torah, he came with proofs from the Torah itself, or gave a reason for the commandment in such a way that the cancelling of the prohibition came from the cancelling of the reason, which in his opinion was not against the intention of the Torah.{v1_12_18:4} And once the Pharisees argued with him because his disciples ate without washing hands and transgressed the words of the Scribes, and he did not protest against them. And he answered them that the statutes of the Scribes are only "a commandment of men learned by rote" [Isaiah 29:13], and God did not command them; but what enters a man's mouth does not defile, only what comes out of it defiles (ibid. 15:11). Now although these words show that he was not strict about all the forbidden foods that the Torah forbade, nevertheless it appears from the end of his words there that his heart did not dare to say so explicitly; on the contrary, he tried to explain his words in such a way that they would not be understood of all forbidden foods. For he said: The evil thoughts go out from the heart and they defile the man, but to eat without washing hands does not defile (ibid. 15:20). We see that he set down a general rule aimed at all forbidden foods and explains it by means of a particular which is only an impurity from the words of the Scribes; and we understand from this that the general rule gives us a slight sense of what was in his heart, and the particular is like an excuse in the face of the complaint. At all events it appears that he refrained as far as possible from appearing as if he wished to uproot anything from the Torah. And therefore his disciples, who did not reach the depth of his mind and did not understand the hidden things of his heart, remained in the position of the Jewish religion with respect to practice. But Paul understood very well the things that were in his heart, and did not fear to bring the thought into action, and what Jesus had hidden in the secret of his heart Paul taught publicly. He said in clear words that from the day that Jesus the Nazarene arose to teach and instruct, the commandments and statutes were abolished, and the merit of a man, whether Jew or non-Jew, depends on faith. And whoever acknowledges the mission of Jesus and his lordship and believes in his resurrection after his death merits eternal good and happiness (Rom. 10:4–11). So he spoke in general terms; and when he speaks of the particular statutes he says absolutely that their observance is not necessary for the members of the faith, and in particular he abolished the commandment of circumcision. And in all these teachings of his he came with proofs from the Holy Scriptures according to the ways of midrash customary in his time.

1.note: The saying on keeping and teaching the commandments is Matt. 5:19; reference kept as printed.

rows.en: These few hints about the deeds of Jesus and his disciples, about the essence of their teaching and their endeavours, will suffice to know the position of this religious society over against the position of the accepted Jewish religion. The system of the first founder, like the system of Paul, was regarded as a danger to the old teaching of the Jews, since both of them contained new beliefs that impaired the accepted faith of Israel. Therefore it is self-evident that the sages of the first generations were compelled to rouse themselves against them and to keep the danger away by means of enactments and decrees, and to make known that the new beliefs and opinions are in contradiction with the Jewish religion. And so enactments came into being, some of which were meant to define the legal status of the Messianists, and in what respect they were to be considered members of the Jewish religion, and some to make a safeguard against their opinions and to warn against being drawn after them. Of the enactments defining their legal status only a little has reached us, but from this little it follows that they were regarded in their eyes as gentiles. Not many days passed before they decreed concerning their slaughtering, their bread and their wine, and that their produce is untithed (Ḥullin 13a), and that meat found in their hands is forbidden and regarded as sacrifices to the dead; and they decreed against intermarrying with them (Tosefta ibid. ch. 2), and that a Torah scroll written by a min is to be burned (Gittin 45b). All these enactments are aimed against the Messianic Jews, for against their followers from the nations they did not need to decree concerning their slaughtering, their bread and their wine, since the prohibition had long been in force. But more numerous are the enactments that they made as a safeguard against their opinions and customs. At first they used to recite the Ten Commandments too in the Shema, and they abolished them because of the complaint of the minim,{v1_12_19:1} so that they should not say that these alone were given to Moses at Sinai (Berakhot 12a, and Yerushalmi ibid.). And indeed it was said thus in the name of Jesus their Messiah, that the chief thing is the Ten Commandments and the commandment of love (Matt. 19:18). This enactment was made in the first century of their era, for R. Nathan, who lived around the middle of the second century, speaks of it as of something enacted in a past time. Further, they enacted because of the minim that "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom for ever and ever" should be said aloud in the Shema (Pesaḥim 56a). The content of this blessing is the acceptance of the kingdom of heaven, and it was instituted by the Zealots, who said that one must accept no yoke of human kingship but only the kingdom of heaven (R. Meir Friedmann in his commentary on Sifre Va-etḥanan 31);{v1_12_19:2} but they said it in a whisper for the sake of peace with the government. Now many of the Pharisees were suspected of heresy (Yerushalmi Berakhot 5:3), and perhaps they found that some of the suspects joined the name of Heaven and the name of Jesus in the whispered acceptance of the kingdom of heaven; therefore they enacted that the acceptance should be said aloud. Around the end of the first century of their era, in the first generation after the destruction of the Temple, they made an addition to the blessing "who humbles the arrogant,"{v1_12_20:1} aimed against the minim, and it is called the blessing of the minim (Berakhot 28b). And they were so strict about saying it that they made it a rule that whoever did not say it is called back, to examine him lest he be a min (Yerushalmi ibid. 5:3). And they decreed that the gilyonim [Gospels] and the books of the minim be burned (Shabbat, Yerushalmi and Bavli ch. 15, and Tosefta ch. 11); and they decreed not to deal with them in disputations and not to be healed by them even for a brief span of life (Avodah Zarah 27b), but to keep as far away from them as possible (Mekhilta Mishpatim with M"S ch. 20;⚠1 Avodah Zarah 17a), because heresy draws the heart (Sifre Shelaḥ 115; Avodah Zarah 27b). They likened it to snares and nets that trap the soul; and in fact several sages were caught in it for moments, as happened to R. Eliezer ben Hyrcanus (Avodah Zarah 17a), and to Ben Dama, the son of R. Ishmael's sister (ibid. 27b), and to Ḥananiah, the nephew of R. Joshua, and to Judah ben Naqosa, and to other sages (Ecclesiastes Rabbah on "All things" and on "And I find"). And every custom of theirs, even one of "what does it matter," was forbidden to the Jews, so as to widen the distance. Such as their custom of slaughtering into a pit in order to let the blood go to waste; for even after they had voted and resolved to abolish the practical commandments, they still held to the commandment of slaughter and warned against eating the blood (Acts 15:20, 29). Against this the sages decreed that one must not slaughter into a pit, because he is doing their statutes, and whoever does so must be examined afterwards (Ḥullin 41a, and Tosefta ibid. ch. 2). And likewise they decreed that one who says, "I will not pass before the ark in coloured garments," may not pass even in white ones; "I will not pass in sandals," he may not pass even barefoot (Megillah 24b); and this is for fear of heresy. For such was the way of the full-fledged Essenes, and they were suspected of heresy (*Bikkurim* I, 183, by R. Simeon Santa).⚠2 It is also related that the minim used to put the tefillin on the forehead and on the palm of the hand, and in the wording of their blessing they used to say, "The good shall bless You" (Megillah ibid.). And they also alluded in their prayer in various ways to their belief in a partnership [in the Godhead], which they called "two powers"; and against every hint of this kind and anything like it the sages were strict with all force (Berakhot 33b), and they strove to show that there is nothing in the proofs that the minim brought them to demonstrate the partnership from the Scriptures. Against the teaching of Paul they warned with extreme warnings. Rabban Simeon ben Gamaliel the Elder had already warned against neglect of the practice, saying (Avot ch. 1): "Not study is the chief thing but practice"; against the view of Paul, who says that merit comes not through practice but through faith. In the Gospels and in the writings of Paul and the apostles we find that they expounded the reasons for the commandments and made the attributes of the Holy One, blessed be He, mercy. Against this the sages stood up and determined that the commandments of the Torah are nothing but decrees.{v1_12_20:2} And it is clear that they determined so with a particular intention. For the sages who were zealous against seeking out the reasons for the commandments are mostly the sages of the first generations after the founding of the Christian religion. One was Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai, who said to his disciples concerning purification by the waters of lustration: "By your life, the dead does not defile and the water does not purify; but the Holy One, blessed be He, said: I have laid down a statute, I have decreed a decree; you are not permitted to transgress My decree" (Numbers Rabbah ch. 19). And likewise R. Eleazar ben Azariah said: "A man should not say, I have no wish for pork, I have no wish for sha'atnez; but [he should say], I do wish it, but my Father in heaven has decreed so upon me, as it is said, 'and I have separated you from the peoples, that you should be Mine' [Leviticus 20:26]; thus he separates himself from transgression and accepts upon himself the yoke of the kingdom of heaven" (Sifra, end of Kedoshim). And likewise we have seen that other Mishnah teachers also determined so (end of Megillah). Against this, we have seen that they themselves expounded the reasons for the commandments, and Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai in particular sought at all times to reveal the spiritual intention in the statutes of the Torah and to expound their reasons.{v1_12_21:1} From this we understand that their warning was aimed only against the seeking of reasons for the purpose of overturning the practice. And therefore the warning was only temporary. Formerly in Israel the sages loved this kind of exposition. So did Hillel, and his disciples saw it from him and did likewise. And now, if a change suddenly appears before our eyes in their view on this point, it is only from the compulsion of events. And when the compelling cause passes, the effect no longer stands; and therefore we find that the very reasons against which they warned (Megillah ibid.) were expounded at a later time without objection (Leviticus Rabbah ch. 27, and in many places). For from the time when the teaching of Paul prevailed, things changed, and the position of the Jews towards the sect of the Christians was not as at first; and from then on they were no longer strict about seeking out the reasons for the commandments. Paul and his party set their faces towards the nations, and to draw their hearts to their teaching they abolished all the practical commandments; and so their teaching changed its character, and in the course of time it became a new teaching that had nothing to do with the teaching of the Jews; most of its people and leaders were gentiles, and from then on the separation was a complete separation. About all these enactments and warnings they were very strict, for they did not regard them as misled but as deniers by will and knowledge, and they called them people who burn their food in public (Berakhot 17b; Sanhedrin 103a). And they said of them that they know their Creator and deny Him (Shabbat 116a, and Yerushalmi ibid.). And of those who know their Master and intend to rebel against Him they said that even if they have so far come only to a small degree of denial, their end is to deny the root principle. Their beginning is that they do not study and do not do, and through this they despise others, and hate the sages, and do not let others do, and deny the commandments that were spoken from Sinai, and the end is that they deny the root principle (Sifra Be-ḥukkotai ch. 2). In short, in their eyes the deeds of this sect did not come from the heart; rather, they thought that their only aim was to throw off the yoke of the Torah; and therefore they called them hypocrites, and hypocrisy and heresy were of equal weight for them. And how harsh are the words they said of them, that they are burners of the world: indeed, if they were given permission they would burn the whole world with its inhabitants in a short moment (Genesis Rabbah ch. 48).

1.note: The abbreviation מ"ס (an edition or commentary?) is unclear; rendered literally.

2.note: Name as printed (סאנטא); transliterated as it stands, identity not checked.

rows.en: We have now passed in review most of the enactments and decrees made with respect to the minim, and most of the warnings that the sages issued, and their harsh judgment of them and of their ways; but there is not a single one of all these that was said, or that is fit to be said, of the members of this sect whose origin is from the nations and who took upon themselves the teaching of the Messianic Jews. Even with slight reflection every discerning person will know the matter correctly: all the sayings mentioned have nothing to do with the Christians among the nations, but are all aimed at the Messianic Jews who lived among them and mostly followed the customs of the Jews; against these was their complaint. From the time when, through Paul's efforts, their teaching became a new teaching that had nothing to do with the teaching of the Jews, and the Messianic Jews dwindled, and the few who remained changed their religion entirely, and most of the members of the religion were from the nations, and its leaders and heads were from them, from that time the Jews no longer had religious enmity against the adherents of the Christian faith. And if their souls grieved over the loss of many of their covenant brethren who went after the new opinions, against this they were consoled⚠1 by the fact that some of the foundations of the Jewish religion, of the principles of righteousness and love and deeds of loving-kindness, and several of their beliefs spread among the nations, and many of the peoples of the earth who formerly worshipped idols and were sunk in corrupt opinions were now drawn to the belief in one God and took up the moral teaching of the Jews. And although they gave the Holy One, blessed be He, a partner, they did not regard this as idolatry (see Sanhedrin 63a, and see there in Tosafot, and Bekhorot 2b in Tosafot). For whoever of the nations believes in the Lord, the God of heaven, even if he associates something else with Him, and keeps the teaching of righteousness between man and his fellow and mercy towards creatures, and guards himself from violence and walks in the ways of morality, has fulfilled, according to the tradition of the Pharisees, the will of God, and kept the Torah and the commandment that the Lord apportioned to the sons of Noah (Sanhedrin 56a), and he is called pious and has a share in the world to come (ibid. 105a). And therefore it was a great satisfaction to the Jews to see that the Torah of Moses had cleared itself a path among the nations, and that a large part of it was accepted by them and they believed in its divinity. And for this reason too they distinguished between the nations in general and the minim among the nations (Avodah Zarah 65a),{v1_12_22:1} and they said explicitly that all the complaint they had against the Messianic Jews was void with respect to the minim among the nations, for these were regarded as resident aliens (ibid., and Ḥullin 13b). In short, it appears that from the time when the Christian religion separated entirely from the Jewish religion, and most of its adherents were from the nations, the Jews had no religious enmity against them. On the contrary, the Jews strove not to give them a pretext for complaint. Thus it is related that at the beginning of the Christian religion there was still a custom in Israel to fast on the first day of the week, and later, when the Christians made the first day of the week a day of rest, the Jews abolished their custom, because they feared the complaint of the Christians, lest they say: because we rejoice on the first day, they fast (Soferim ch. 16). From that time the blessing of the minim no longer had a place; therefore they changed its wording and set it against the informers. And if the first Christians looked on this blessing with an evil eye and thought that it was aimed against them, they were misled at all times by informers; for against the minim among the nations the Jews had no religious enmity. Rather, the enlightened among the Jews saw at all times in the spread of the ideas of the Torah among the nations the first step towards the fulfilment of the exalted promise that the day will come when all the inhabitants of the world will recognize the true unity, "and the Lord shall be one, and His name one" [Zechariah 14:9]. But the narrowness of eye and baseless hatred of individuals caused a delay in the matter, and the hope of the good has not yet come; for instead of compromise and peace they thought at all times to uproot the Jewish religion like a tree, and "the daughter rose up against her mother" [Micah 7:6]. Yet not the daughter, but the members of her household, were incensed against the children of the mother. But vain is the counsel of man. For the mother, though old, has not ceased to give her strength; still, like a fresh native tree, "she bears fruit in old age" [Psalms 92:15]. And better than those who came after him did Jesus their Messiah understand the matter, when he spoke of the eternity of our Torah, saying: Even heaven and earth shall pass away and change, but not one letter of the Torah shall fall to the ground.

1.note: Read as הופסה (from הפיס דעת, 'appeased'), as with הפסת דעת on the next page.

footnotes.en: He expounds and says: If it was said to the ancients, "You shall not murder," and whoever kills a person is liable to death, I say to you that even one who provokes his fellow is liable to judgment, and whoever calls his fellow wicked, and whoever shames his fellow and calls him a fool, falls into Gehenna (Matt. 5:21–22). These are a fence for "You shall not murder"; and so the Pharisees made a fence and said: Whoever gains honour through the disgrace of his fellow has no share in the world to come (Yerushalmi Ḥagigah ch. 2; Megillah 28a). And whoever calls his fellow wicked, [the other] may go down with him into his livelihood⚠1 (Kiddushin 28a); and whoever shames his fellow in public is as if he sheds blood (Bava Metzia 58b), and it is better for him to throw himself into a fiery furnace (ibid. 59a), and he has no share in the world to come (Avot ch. 3). For "You shall not commit adultery" he makes a fence, that even one who looks at a woman is called an adulterer (ibid. 5:27); and this is a fence of the sages, that one should not look at women, nor be alone with a woman, nor talk much with her, nor converse with her in the street. And for the commandment of divorce he made a fence, that a man should not divorce his wife unless he found in her "something indecent" (ibid. 5:32), and this is the exposition of Beit Shammai (Gittin ch. 9). For "You shall not take [the name in vain]" he made a fence, that a man should not swear at all, in line with the Essenes, who refrained from swearing. And in his saying that it is fitting that speech alone should suffice, without an oath, so that it be "yes, yes" and "no, no" (ibid. 5:37), this is the teaching of the Pharisees word for word (Sifra Kedoshim ch. 8; Bava Metzia 49a). According to his saying about fulfilment, it appears that he meant that he came to add, as we have explained; and accordingly the old reading in the Talmud (Shabbat 116b), "I came not to take away [from the Torah of Moses], I came to add," is the correct one, and not as the emendation of the corrector, "and not"; and perhaps one should read "but".

1.note: Idiom of Kiddushin 28a: the insulted man may harm the other's livelihood.

footnotes.en: "What is hateful to you," etc., is an ancient proverb (Tobit 6),⚠1 and Hillel called it the whole of the Torah, "and the rest is commentary" (Shabbat 31a). Deeds of loving-kindness are a pillar of the world (Avot ch. 1). "You shall love your neighbour as yourself" is a great principle (Sifra Kedoshim ch. 4). "With the measure with which a man judges, they judge him" (Matt. 7:2); its counterpart: "Judge every man in the scale of merit" (Avot ch. 1), and "Whoever judges his fellow in the scale of merit is judged favourably" (Shabbat 127b). "Whoever forgives the transgressions of his brother is forgiven" (ibid. 6:14); its counterpart: "Whoever passes over his [right to] retribution, all his transgressions are passed over" (Yoma 23a). And his commandment to give charity in secret (ibid. 6:1–4) is found among the Pharisees (Ḥagigah 5a; Shekalim 5:6; Bava Batra 9b; Sifre Re'eh 116). Loving-kindness towards an enemy is found in Holy Scripture (Exodus 23:4–5; Proverbs 25), and Scripture says: "You shall not take vengeance nor bear a grudge" [Leviticus 19:18], "You shall not hate your brother in your heart" [Leviticus 19:17]. And Hillel says: "Love the creatures and bring them near to the Torah." They deliberately did not speak of this in particular, for by law no Israelite is to be an enemy to an Israelite, as it is said, "You shall not hate your brother in your heart"; and how could they command about something that is impossible according to the law?

1.note: The saying is Tobit 4:15; the chapter figure in the scan reads ו' (or ד'), kept as printed.

footnotes.en: "[I dwell] with the contrite," etc. (Isaiah 57); "The meek shall inherit the earth" (Psalms 37); "Whoever humbles himself, the Holy One, blessed be He, raises him up" (Eruvin 13b); "humble," etc., "is a son of the world to come" (Sanhedrin 88b). "He who works righteousness shall dwell in the tent of the Lord" (Psalms 15). "Whoever has mercy on creatures receives mercy from heaven" (Shabbat 151b). "The pure of heart ascend the mountain of the Lord" (Psalms 24). "Lovers of peace are called children of the Omnipresent" (Sifre Re'eh 96). "God seeks the pursued" (Ecclesiastes Rabbah 3). "The insulted are the beloved of the Lord" (Shabbat 88b). And there is no need of proof that the belief of the Jews from of old was that the mercies of the Lord are upon the nations as upon Israel, as is explained in the chapter before this one. But just as the Jews in his time believed that the love of the Holy One, blessed be He, is special to Israel, so too was his belief (Matt. 15:26, and in many places).
Of all these principles we find examples: Sifre Ekev 49; Mekhilta Va-yassa ch. 2; Sotah 48b; and see Beitzah 16a; Sotah 8a, and in many places; Avot 1:4;⚠1 Sotah 3b.

1.note: Serving not to receive a reward is Avot 1:3; kept as printed.

footnotes.en: He did not describe his concept of the kingdom of heaven explicitly, and he did not need to explain it, for he was speaking with Jews, and they knew that the hoped-for repair of the world under the kingdom of heaven is that the idols will be cut off, and all flesh will call upon His name, and the wicked will turn to the Lord, and all the inhabitants of the world will accept the yoke of His kingdom (the Aleinu prayer).

"The Sabbath is handed over to you, and you are not handed over to the Sabbath" (Mekhilta Ki Tissa; Mark 2:27). "Whoever hears a little is made to hear much" (ibid. Va-yassa ch. 1; Matt. 13:12). "As I [teach] freely, so you [teach] freely" (Bekhorot 29a; ibid. 10:8). "It is enough for the servant to be like his master" (Berakhot 58b; Tosefta Sanhedrin ch. 13; ibid. 10:25). "Your deeds will bring you near and your deeds will push you away" (Eduyot ch. 4;⚠1 ibid. 12:37). "Whoever humbles himself, the Holy One, blessed be He, raises him up," etc. (Eruvin 13b; ibid. 4:15).⚠2 "The Messiah comes only when attention is diverted" (Sanhedrin 97a; ibid. 24:44). And his parable of the splinter and the beam (Arakhin 16b; ibid. 7:3), and of the householder who hired labourers (Yerushalmi Berakhot ch. 3;⚠3 ibid. 20:1). All this is a little out of much: one can show examples in the books of the Oral Torah for most of his sayings, or of those attributed to him. And needless to say, the sages did not copy his words, for we know⚠4 how careful they were not to hear a word or half a word touching on heresy. And although several of the sayings we have cited were said by later Tannaim, this is no proof at all that they are not ancient; for we find several sayings that are clearly ancient and are found in Ben Sira or in another ancient book, and they are said word for word in the name of later Tannaim, not because these founded them but because they were current in their mouths.

2.note: In Matthew the saying is 23:12 (cf. 18:4); kept as printed.

3.note: The parable is in Yerushalmi Berakhot 2:8; the scan reads פ"ג.

4.note: Printed ברעתנו; read בדעתנו, 'as we know'.

footnotes.en: Once his disciples were plucking ears of grain on the Sabbath, and the Pharisees rebuked him because he did not protest against them; and he answered them that this is permitted by law when a man has nothing to eat, and the proof is from David, who ate holy bread in time of need, and the priests do work in the Temple on the Sabbath (Matt. 12:2–5). And the sum of the matter: "The Sabbath is handed over to you, and you are not handed over to the Sabbath" (Mark 2:27). He also said that divorce is to be abolished, and gave the reason that from the beginning the Holy One, blessed be He, appointed that the bond of marriage should be a lasting bond that may never be dissolved; Moses in his time⚠1 was compelled to permit divorce to them because of their stiff-neckedness (Matt. 19:8).

1.note: Second word blurred in the scan; read בזמנו.

footnotes.en: The reason they were called minim is that they called themselves "believers" [ma'aminim] (Acts 4:32, and in many places), and the Jews called them by a word that plays on that word, minim (*Musaf he-Arukh*, s.v. min),⚠1 a name by which they had also called from of old another religious sect, which believed in two powers.

1.note: Abbreviation unclear in the scan; read as Musaf he-Arukh.

footnotes.en: It seems to me that the words "our God, King of the universe," which are said in every blessing, were added at a later time, namely at the time when the sect of the Zealots arose and said that one must not accept the kingship of flesh and blood but only the kingship of heaven. But among the ancients the blessing was without [mention of] kingship, as in "Blessed are You, O Lord, teach me Your statutes" [Psalms 119:12]; and likewise in the Eighteen Benedictions there is no mention of kingship, nor is there any mention of it in the closing formula of each and every blessing. And therefore several sages were not strict about saying kingship.

See what I wrote in *Bikkurim* 5624 [1864], p. 92, where I proved from the Tosefta, which says "and includes that of the minim in 'who humbles the arrogant'," that "who humbles the arrogant" is ancient and that they made an addition to it against the minim. And in Yerushalmi Ta'anit ch. 2 and Berakhot ch. 4 it says: "If a man says to you, they are seventeen, say to him: that of the minim they already fixed at Yavneh." The meaning is that "the Shoot [of David]" was late (see Numbers Rabbah and Tanḥuma Koraḥ), having been enacted after the blessing of the minim; and therefore, if the blessing of the minim had also been entirely new, they would come to only seventeen. To this he says that that of the minim was fixed at Yavneh, meaning that they fixed it in "who humbles the arrogant," and so the number comes out right. Accordingly, at first the prayer for redemption was included in the first blessing, "and brings a redeemer," etc., and in the seventh blessing, "and redeem us speedily," etc., and in the tenth blessing, "Sound the great shofar"; and the kingdom of the house of David was not mentioned. Later they included that of David in "who builds Jerusalem," that is, they added: "and speedily establish the throne of David within it"; while the main passage of the blessing was "and build it," etc., "an everlasting building," and to this the closing "who builds Jerusalem" is fitting. And at a still later time they enacted "the Shoot"; and both of these were against the minim, who said that the son of David had already come.

See Yerushalmi and Bavli, end of Megillah. The words of the Yerushalmi: "Those who translate, 'My people, children of Israel, as we are merciful in heaven, so you shall be merciful on earth: a cow or a ewe, it and its young you shall not slaughter both on one day'" [Leviticus 22:28]. And in Leviticus Rabbah ch. 27 and Deuteronomy Rabbah Ki Tetze they expounded the reasons for these commandments thus. And see what I write below in the text, and *Tosafot Yom Tov* on Megillah ch. 5.⚠1 And R. Simeon Santa⚠2 wrote sensible words on this subject in *Bikkurim* I, p. 183.
